Latest Update: Trouble at Mars: NASA's Perseverance rover, Odyssey orbiter halt science work due to glitches

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two of NASA's Mars explorers are sidelined by glitches at the moment.
  • The Perseverance rover and Mars Odyssey orbiter have stood down from science work due to technical problems, NASA announced on Thursday (Nov.
  • Perseverance has been sidelined by an antenna glitch, and the venerable Odyssey is dealing with a balky reaction wheel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two of NASA's Mars explorers are sidelined by glitches at the moment.

The Perseverance rover and Mars Odyssey orbiter have stood down from science work due to technical problems, NASA announced on Thursday (Nov. 19).

Perseverance has been sidelined by an antenna glitch, and the venerable Odyssey is dealing with a balky reaction wheel. NASA hopes both can get back to work at Mars by the end of November.

Perseverance landed inside Mars' Jezero Crater in February 2021, tasked with assessing the area's potential to support past life and with collecting dozens of samples for future return to Earth.

It has done all this and more. The Perseverance team has determined that Jezero hosted a potentially habitable lake billions of years ago. And the car-sized rover has found a wealth of complex organic compounds in Martian rock, some of which might themselves be signs of life (though assessing this hypothesis fully will likely require bringing Perseverance's samples to Earth for analysis, scientists stress).

In addition, Perseverance just set a new distance record for off-Earth driving, rolling past the mark set by its smaller cousin, NASA's Opportunity rover (28.06 miles, or 45.16 kilometers).

Perseverance broke that record on Oct. 11. Just 19 days later, however, the mission team noticed a problem: The rover's main UHF downlink radio — which it uses to send information home to Earth, via data-relay satellites in Mars orbit — failed to send its usual "heartbeat" pings to the main computer.

Perseverance detected this problem autonomously and reacted as it was programmed to do: The six-wheeled robot switched to its backup UHF radio and went into a protective "safe mode," shutting down all non-essential systems.

The rover team recovered Perseverance from safe mode but soon noticed another issue: "The backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output," NASA officials wrote in an update on Thursday.

Perseverance's handlers have stopped using that backup radio as well; the rover is now communicating with Earth directly (without the help of relay orbiters), sending signals to NASA's Deep Space Network dishes via its high-gain antenna.

Sources indicate that this pathway features lower data rates, and the mission team wants to prioritize the delivery of diagnostic information. So they've paused Perseverance's science work, which includes observations by its various cameras.

The glitch may be disappointing to devoted Perseverance fans, many of whom have already noticed that the mission website hasn't uploaded any newly introduced raw images since Nov. 7. But there's no reason to panic, according to NASA.

"The rover is stable and communicating with the team," agency officials wrote in Thursday's update. "The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November, and NASA will provide further updates in the future as the team works the problem.".

Mars Odyssey's problem may be more serious: The orbiter, which arrived at the Red Planet in October 2001, recently lost the use of one of its reaction wheels.

According to recent reports, odyssey has four reaction wheels, which help the spacecraft maintain its orientation in space. Three of the four must be functional to do this job, and Odyssey already lost a reaction wheel in 2013.

This latest problem cropped up on Nov. 4, when Odyssey went into safe mode. The orbiter stayed in this protective posture until Nov. 6 while mission team members diagnosed and dealt with the problem. They've made some progress, at one point getting the faulty wheel to move when commanded.

"Further testing is being conducted to confirm whether the wheel is recoverable," NASA officials wrote in Thursday's update.

Though it has been out of safe mode for two weeks, Odyssey still has not resumed its science or data-relay work. (The orbiter has long helped NASA's Mars surface craft send information home to Earth.).

"The goal is for Odyssey to return to science and relay operations at the conclusion of these tests and analysis during the last week of November, and NASA will provide future updates on status and timeline as the team learns more," agency officials wrote in the patch.

In a recent development, if the reaction wheel, isn't recoverable, Odyssey's days are numbered. The mission team will have to orient the orbiter solely using its thrusters, and Odyssey has enough hydrazine fuel left to do this for a just month or two, according to NASA.

According to recent reports, odyssey's mission has been a rousing success, no matter what happens with the reaction wheel. The orbiter has operated at Mars longer than any other spacecraft, and it has made a number of important scientific contributions.

"Odyssey created the first global maps detailing the composition of the Martian surface, which have become foundational for Mars geologists," NASA officials wrote in Thursday's update.

"The orbiter's surface maps have also played a key role in identifying hazards at landing sites, spotting locations of scientific interest for landers and rovers to explore, and mapping water molecules in the top 3 feet (1 meter) of the surface, including buried ice that could be useful to the first astronauts on Mars.".

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • SHOF board members Fletcher Foster (chairman of SHOF’s Nashville Committee), Mike O’Neill and Jon Platt made the induction to Miller’s widow, Mary Miller.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that roger Miller, the witty wordsmith who delivered hits as “Dang Me” and “King of the Road,” was posthumously inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame, it was declared on Monday (Nov. 23). Miller, who died in 1992 at age 56, was honored during an intimate ceremony held on Nov. 17 at BMI headquarters in Nashville, prior to the BMI Country Awards.

SHOF board members Fletcher Foster (chairman of SHOF’s Nashville Committee), Mike O’Neill and Jon Platt made the induction to Miller’s widow, Mary Miller.

According to recent reports, “We were ecstatic to learn that Roger was being inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame,” Mary Miller said in a statement. “Of all his many talents, he was most proud of his songwriting. This lifetime achievement would have meant a great deal to him, and we are honored to celebrate the recognition of his extraordinary body of work.”.

According to recent reports, the annual SHOF Induction & Awards Gala in Fresh York City each June does not usually include posthumous inductions, but the organization has taken to hosting posthumous inductions at special events to recognize songwriters they missed during their lifetimes. In the past two years, Prince, Cindy Walker, Hugo Peretti & Luigi Creatore, Bert Berns, Jerry Ragovoy and Donna Summer have been inducted into the SHOF posthumously in this way.

It has been revealed that miller had 11 top 10 hits on Billboard’s Hot Country Songs chart in the 1960s, all but one of which he wrote or co-wrote. He had long runs at No. 1 with “Dang Me” in 1964 and “King of the Road” in 1965. Both songs won Grammys for best country and western song, a term that was phased out in favor of country in 1969. Both of these songs also made the top 10 on the all-genre Billboard Hot 100, as did three other Miller hits: “Chug-a-Lug,” “Engine Engine #9” and “England Swings.”.

“King of the Road,” which received Grammy nominations for both record and song of the year, is one of the most famous country songs from the 1960s.

Miller won 11 Grammys in just two years (1965 and 1966). In 1966, he became the first artist from any genre to win six Grammys in one year. “Dang Me” and “King of the Road” have both been voted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.

Miller received five awards from the Academy of Country Music Awards, including single record of the year in 1969 for his country version of Bobby Russell’s song “Little Green Apples” (which O.C. Smith popularized in the pop market). Miller’s other ACM Awards are songwriter of the year and man of the year in 1966, the pioneer award in 1988 and the ACM Poet’s award in 2012.

Miller was voted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame (no relationship to the SHOF) in 1973 and the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1995.

Miller was also a popular TV personality, frequently appearing on variety and talk reveals and starring in his own NBC series, The Roger Miller Show, in 1966.

Miller wrote the music and lyrics for Big River, a musical adaptation of Mark Twain’s The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. Big River won seven Tonys in 1985, including best musical. Miller received both a Tony for best original score and the Drama Desk Award for outstanding lyrics.

Recent findings suggest that subsequent generations of artists have continued to record Miller’s songs and achieve top rankings on Hot Country Songs. Ricky Van Shelton reached No. 1 in 1988 with a remake of Miller’s 1970 song “Don’t We All Have the Right.” Dwight Yoakam reached No. 7 in 1992 with “It Only Hurts When I Cry,” which Yoakam cowrote with Miller. Alan Jackson took “Tall, Tall Trees,” which Miller cowrote with George Jones, to No. 1 in 1995. Brooks & Dunn’s reached No. 1 in 1988 with a new version of Miller’s 1966 hit “Husbands and Wives.” Though it was decades old at that point, Miller’s song was nominated for song of the year at both the CMA Awards and the ACM Awards in 1999.

CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1458 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that after more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles.
  • The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
  • Recent findings suggest that the elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that after more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The long-awaited result could help scientists investigate a largely unexplored realm of physics where unknown particles and forces of nature may exist.

The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Researchers at the University of Manchester played notable roles in the international effort, contributing to the advanced technology that made the measurement possible.

Recent findings suggest that the elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. That is strong enough to qualify as evidence, but physicists will need additional data before they can officially declare a discovery. Even so, the finding marks a major milestone in a search that has lasted more than 40 years.

It also creates fresh opportunities to test the Standard Model, the leading scientific framework describing fundamental particles and how they interact. By examining this exceptionally rare decay in greater detail, researchers hope to uncover subtle clues that could eventually point toward physics beyond our current understanding.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal New Physics.

It has been revealed that the LHCb experiment specializes in studying particles that contain beauty quarks. These are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that make up much of the ordinary matter around us.

It has been revealed that when particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider, enormous numbers of beauty quarks are produced. However, they survive for only about one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying into other particles.

In a recent development, scientists study these transformations because they may reveal the influence of particles that cannot be directly observed at the collider. By measuring exactly how frequently different decays occur, physicists can search for unexpected effects that might indicate previously unknown physics.

Particularly rare decays offer an vital advantage. Because they happen so infrequently, their rates can be especially sensitive to contributions from undiscovered particles. Even small differences between predicted and observed decay rates could provide valuable evidence of new forces or particles.

A One in 10 Billion Particle Decay.

It has been revealed that the newly observed signal involves a process known as 'Bd to mu mu'. During this decay, a particle containing a beauty quark transforms into two muons, which are heavier relatives of electrons.

According to theoretical predictions, this transformation should occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. Despite decades of investigation, no individual experiment had previously produced convincing evidence that it occurs.

The upgraded LHCb experiment has now achieved a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. Although this meets the standard for reporting evidence, particle physicists generally require a significance of five sigma before announcing a confirmed discovery.

Professor Chris Parkes, Head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, led the international LHCb collaboration during construction of its major upgrade. He also oversaw the collaboration's approval of the newly introduced findings.

He explained: "The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking -- a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.

"The UK made the largest national contribution to the project, pioneering new technologies that have made today's result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start; we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale.".

Parkes, who became a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year in recognition of his contributions to LHCb, offered a memorable comparison to illustrate just how improbable the decay is.

"This decay is remarkably unlikely; the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth.".

Advanced LHC Detectors Make the Breakthrough Possible.

Detecting such an uncommon event requires instruments capable of following the movements of particles with extraordinary accuracy.

According to recent reports, one of the most notable components of the upgraded LHCb experiment is a silicon pixel detector developed with major contributions from researchers in the United Kingdom. Called the Vertex Locator, it measures the paths of particles generated during collisions inside the collider.

Positioned just five millimeters from the LHC beams, the detector allows researchers to determine precisely where particles originate and where they subsequently decay.

In a recent development, dr. Stefano De Capua, who directed detector construction at the University of Manchester, described the extensive collaboration behind the technology.

"We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons.".

The wider LHCb upgrade also allows the experiment to gather information at up to five times its previous rate. This greater capacity, together with improvements in tracking technology, is helping physicists identify events that were previously too difficult to measure reliably.

Exploring the Mysterious Zeptoverse.

Beyond confirming an exceptionally rare particle process, the result could help scientists investigate what they call the 'Zeptoverse'.

This name refers to an almost unimaginably small scale, measured in zeptometers. A single zeptometer is just a billionth of a trillionth of a meter. Physicists suspect that effects from presently unknown particles and forces could become apparent when nature is examined at these extreme scales.

For now, the upcoming measurement agrees with the Standard Model. Researchers have not found evidence that the established theory is wrong, but increasingly precise measurements could reveal deviations that current experiments cannot yet detect.

Such differences would be especially significant because they could indicate where the Standard Model stops providing a complete explanation of the physical world.

Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, who serves as Deputy Physics Coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, emphasized the importance of finally obtaining the long-sought signal.

"There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of fresh physics from beyond our current knowledge.

Industry observers note that "The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data.".

What Comes Next for CERN's Particle Research?

The upgraded LHCb experiment is expected to continue gathering a substantially larger collection of measurements into the early 2030s. With more data, physicists should be able to determine the frequency of this rare decay with much greater precision.

Researchers are also planning another major upgrade that could increase data collection rates by an additional factor of ten. This would improve their ability to investigate extremely rare particle processes and search for the effects of unknown particles at even smaller distance scales.

Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who did not participate in the experiment, highlighted how improvements in scientific instruments can lead to key advances in understanding nature.

According to recent reports, "This is an vital result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments, and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don't understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing -- that's science! LHCb is a major scientific success.".

The experiment receives funding from the Science and Technology Facilities Council, which operates within UK Research and Innovation. The UK LHCb collaboration brings together scientists from ten universities across the United Kingdom and the STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory.

It has been revealed that although the newly detected decay has not yet revealed any unknown particles or forces, it gives physicists a powerful new way to search for them. After more than 40 years of effort, an extraordinarily elusive process is finally becoming accessible to detailed study, potentially bringing researchers closer to understanding some of the universe's deepest mysteries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It hasn't even been a week yet but avid Grand Theft Auto VI fans the world over have been exploring every nook and cranny of Leonidas, the fictional state (based on Florida) in which all the action is set, and unsurprisingly, since this is a Rockstar game, there have been some incredibly cool Easter eggs discovered already.

Here's a list of some of the standout discoveries but please be warned: some of these posts contain story spoilers, so if you want to go in fresh, experiencing everything for yourself first, stop reading now.

Sea monsters have long been a part of GTA lore, but no one has yet found a living one in GTA VI ….

Dexter Morgan's iconic Florida apartment and kill room setup, replicated for fans of the show.

He's just as tough to track down in the game as in real life.

There are more than a few haunting discoveries to be made in Leonidas.

Fans lost their minds at this Arthur Morgan sighting.

Imagine seeing this for the first time.

This is a terrifying glimpse into a legendary video game nightmare.

Wander too far into the wood and you might witness a tractor beam.

In a recent development, this is just a small sample of what players have already discovered, but you should expect many more cool callbacks and Easter eggs to be unearthed as players get to spend even more time exploring Rockstar's incredible world.
